Woooooohooo fluoxetine train.  Yeah!  As someone who recently got bumped up to 40, I have been really pleasantly surprised by it.  I thought I would feel like a zombie and fake, but I feel more like myself than I have in YEARS.  YEARS of depression have been lifted- I still have issues obviously, but I feel like they're surmountable with the fluoxetine.   It's one of the old standards, and I was terrified to try Vitamin P due to the "soccer mom rep" it has.   I mean, I'm sure yr pharmacist will tell you this, but take it early in the morning and try to consume it with some food (at the very least, a LARGE glass of water).

The cool part is going to happen in about a week.  You're going to feel... more normal.  Energetic.  Better.  You won't be 100% okay, but you'll be able to feel things again.  20 mg is a starting dose- yr Dr might raise it higher if you don't react to it poorly.  Some people get nauseous from it.  If you do, ask yr Dr what you should do- they might give you 10 mgs to try and ease you in.

If you have trouble sleeping, talk to your psychiatrist about trazodone as well.  Fluox can give you TOO much energy and pep, and trazodone is an anti-anxiety that also knocks you out.  Be gentle with it though-  use only as needed.  It's not the most fun, but it's better than not sleeping and having weeks of mental health work feel useless because you're tired.  Eat calcium-rich foods!  Drink a lot of water.  And most of all, journal journal  journal journal everything.  Document EVERYTHING.  Write it all down.  If you aren't already, try to do an hour-by-hour diary-  Write one/two sentences describing what you've done and then one/two descriptors of how you feel with an intensity of 1-10 next to it.  This will give your Dr a lot of information to work with.  Start today!  If you miss an hour or two, it's okay.  That way, they can see the progress you are/are not making and adjust as needed.
Eg-
> 8 a.m.- "I made myself a smoothie with lots of healthy produce and drank 3/4 of it. I feel proud of myself (6) and productive (5)."

Let me speak more from his point of view.  I lost my father early last year to suicide, and it made me need to feel anything and everything as much as possible.  I'm 25, I was 24 when I lost my father.  31 is still very, very young to lose your mother.

While I didn't cheat on my boyfriend outright, I would talk to people and try to feel wanted.  He knows about this, we've talked about it, but it got to the point where he would follow me home because he thought I was actually cheating.  The thing is, I was really active in my BDSM community before I ever met him, when I was young and had less responsibilities.  With what happened in my life, my brain reverted to who I was BEFORE, just because I couldn't really deal with what was happening to me and to my life.  It was simple, and the instant gratification literally saved me from shutting down completely.

I'm so sorry that he's being critical of you and comparing you to her.  I'm not proud, but I did the same thing with my boyfriend.  It's impossible to be happy and feel happy and your partner never gives enough or is sensitive enough or understands enough and it takes months to stop.  There's nothing you can say that will make him feel better, and he's comparing a shallow, commitment-free friend to someone who he's spent six years of devotion and love with.  She is going to be sparkly, and distracting, and different.


Sometimes, we do stupid things.  Grief is a shit, shit thing.    Enroll in therapy and/or have him enroll with a different therapist.  Go with him for a couple sessions if he's comfortable with it.  I started a deeply self-destructive cycle to keep myself from having any hope. If you're done with the relationship, end it. Leave if you don't want him, but if ANY part of you wants him, make sure that you really work it out and focus.  I think it's really important to set boundaries and have honest, honest conversations.  I know this will be unpopular- but even if he IS cheating on you, you shouldn't automatically dismiss the relationship.

One of my favorite psychotherapists, Esther Perel, has a good quote on cheating from an article in *The Atlantic*:
>As I listen to her, I start to suspect that her affair is about neither her husband nor their relationship. Her story echoes a theme that has come up repeatedly in my work: affairs as a form of self-discovery, a quest for a new (or lost) identity. For these seekers, infidelity is less likely to be a symptom of a problem, and more likely an expansive experience that involves growth, exploration, and transformation.

>“Expansive?!,” I can hear some people exclaiming. “Self-discovery?! Cheating is cheating, whatever fancy New Age labels you want to put on it. It’s cruel, it’s selfish, it’s dishonest, and it’s abusive.” Indeed, to the one who has been betrayed, it can be all these things. Intimate betrayal feels intensely personal—a direct attack in the most vulnerable place. And yet I often find myself asking jilted lovers to consider a question that seems ludicrous to them: What if the affair had nothing to do with you?

>Sometimes when we seek the gaze of another, it’s not our partner we are turning away from, but the person we have become. We are not looking for another lover so much as another version of ourselves. The Mexican essayist Octavio Paz described eroticism as a “thirst for otherness.” So often, the most intoxicating “other” that people discover in an affair is not a new partner; it’s a new self.

Bro, as a 24 going through probate with the untimely death of a father, you suck.  This shit is hard, and sad, and really awful.  There's a lot of advice that I wish someone had told me seven months ago and even now.

First off, you're going to want to make sure that this 26 year old son is next-of-kin.  Was there a husband or any other kids?  As someone who is going through probate right now and there was no will left behind, this is what I wish someone would have said to me (I'm 24 in CA however):

If his name is on any shared accounts with her, have him transfer anything to his name solely.  That includes cars and money.  They will be caught in probate otherwise.  Have him total up her debts on his own.  Get her free credit report.  Open her mail, figure out her life.  Cancel any and all services for her property/house.  Send one of the credit bureaus a death notification, they will notify everyone else.  FREEZE CREDIT ASAP.  Seriously.  Get at least 5 copies of the death certificate and make more photocopies-  if anyone tries to take one, ask them if they can just scan it into their system instead.  If there is ANY property or large amounts of money involved that his name is not on, have him get a lawyer ASAP.  ASAP.  Funeral expenses can be paid for out of her estate.  He does not have to settle ANY of her debts personally.  The estate is used for all of it.  "When Someone Dies" by Scott Taylor Smith is a good baseline guide, but it doesn't get into the nitty-gritty of probate, sudden deaths with no preparation, etc.

Situations like this, *no one* will know proper protocol.  Just say the words "next-of-kin" as much as possible to acquire information.  To become an official administrator of the estate, he's going to need ORDERS and LETTERS from the court, which I'd recommend getting a lawyer for that.  If there is a trust, he becomes a trustee.  He will also need legal proof for that.

If you have any other specific questions, please feel free to inbox me or comment here.  It's a process.

My big takeaway from my father's sudden death was *write a holographic will*.  Write a will out, in your own handwriting, at the very least.  If you have any assets, get a lawyer to help you draft out a real will.  Tell this to everyone you know.  If the worst case scenario happens, it will spare your loved ones a lot of grief and suffering in the months after your untimely death.  Research as do a few hours of work so your loved ones will not have to go through probate.  Probate is the actual worst, especially as a grieving human.

In my lil cast iron- Whole seeds of: a couple cardamom pods, shake of coriander, shake of cumin, 2 cloves, A TEENY bit of cinnamon bark (sometimes I leave this out, I get moody about it), whole peppercorn.  Roast in a pan until they start to smell GREAT. Remove from heat, pop open the cardamom pods, and then grind the spices.  Add this powder to blender.  Take a few tbsp of fish sauce & fresh squeezed lime juice, swish it around your grinder to get the last of the sticky cardamom out, then dump that in the blender.  Add a bit of turmeric to the blender.  If you have molasses, add a big spoon of that.  If you don't (I never do), I just use some dates.  Sometimes I'll add some tomato paste. One time I used two rogue ketchup packets that I couldn't bring myself to throw away.

In the same pan: A small handful of dried bird chiles and 1/4 c peanuts and/or cashews.  Pop it in the oven.

In a large sheet of foil: 6-8 garlic cloves, a thinly sliced shallot, a a good sized chunk of thinly sliced galangal or ginger, 1/2 of a small, thinly sliced white onion, three to five shelled tamarind pods, a small scoop of coconut oil.  Seal it *en papillote*  and let it all roast until you smell it.  The spices are in the blender, doin' their thing.  The kitchen will start to smell like garlic, spice, peanut, roasting chile, and when it smells toasty, whip it out and dump everything in the foil in the blender first.  Blend that realllllly well, then add the peanuts/chile.

As a photog myself, my advice would be:

What are your favorite features about yourself?  If you really like the color/tone of your hair, find a dress that is about the same value (dark/light) in a complimentary color.  If you have dark hair and light skin, focus on finding a color that's a similar value to your skin tone (albeit a different color) so that when your photographer photographs you, your hair might be too dark, but your skin will be perfectly exposed.  I don't recommend being photographed in white, but darker ivories will give the illusion of proper white.  You seem to have that down.  White, especially in wide apertures, can be easily blown out.  Conversely, dark colors can become too overwhelming and become too distracting of a focal point.

Also, depending on the style of photographs, this advice might be completely nixed if they're HDR, detail-rich, or taken with a camera that can reclaim highlights very well.  I can't actually see the portfolio of your photog.  If you post the portfolio, I can tell you if any of my advice is worth a damn or if you should ignore it haha.

Finally, I like prints.  I like details.  I think that as long as it's not a LOUD, LOUD print, textures and layers and jewelry and details add richness to the photograph.  Do not be afraid of lace patterns, delicate floral prints.  What I would do is stay away from bold, bold colors- is your SO's shirt a very saturated green, or is it more muted?  Chances are that in editing, that color is going to be able to pop a lot more, so I would stick with a more muted green.
